content: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is a hormone produced by the placenta following implantation. It is commonly detected in pregnancy tests, such as hCG pregnancy strip tests. However, certain cancerous tumors can also produce hCG, and elevated levels in non-pregnant individuals may indicate malignancy or paraneoplastic syndromes. It remains unclear whether hCG production in these cases is a cause or an effect of carcinogenesis. The pituitary gland produces a hormone analogous to hCG, known as luteinizing hormone (LH), in both males and females across all age groups. Endogenous forms of hCG can be categorized and measured in various ways, including total hCG, C-terminal peptide total hCG, intact hCG, free β-subunit hCG, β-core fragment hCG, hyperglycosylated hCG, nicked hCG, alpha hCG, and pituitary hCG. Pharmaceutical preparations of hCG are derived from either animal or synthetic sources. These include medically justified gonadotropin preparations and others of questionable validity. As of December 6, 2011, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has banned the sale of homeopathic and over-the-counter hCG diet products, deeming them fraudulent and illegal. Structurally, hCG is a heterodimeric glycoprotein composed of an alpha (α) subunit, identical to that of LH, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), and a unique beta (β) subunit. The α subunit consists of 92 amino acids, with most of its outer amino acids being hydrophilic. Function hCG interacts with the LHCG receptor in the ovary, promoting the maintenance of the corpus luteum during early pregnancy. This ensures the secretion of progesterone, which enriches the uterine lining with blood vessels and capillaries to sustain the developing fetus. Due to its highly negative charge, hCG may repel maternal immune cells, protecting the fetus during the first trimester. It has also been hypothesized that hCG facilitates local maternal immunotolerance, as hCG-treated endometrial cells can induce T cell apoptosis. This suggests a role in peritrophoblastic immune tolerance and trophoblast invasion, which supports fetal development in the endometrium. hCG levels have been linked to the severity of morning sickness or hyperemesis gravidarum in pregnant women. Clinically, hCG is used to induce ovulation in the ovaries and stimulate testosterone production in the testes due to its similarity to LH. It is often extracted from the urine of pregnant women for use in fertility treatments. hCG also plays a role in cellular differentiation and proliferation and may activate apoptosis. Production Naturally, hCG is produced in the human placenta by syncytiotrophoblast cells. It can be extracted from the urine of pregnant women or produced using recombinant DNA technology in genetically modified cell cultures. Commercial preparations such as Pregnyl, Profasi, and Novarel are derived from urine, while Ovidrel is produced using recombinant DNA technology. hCG Forms Endogenous hCG exists in various forms, including total hCG, intact hCG, free β-subunit hCG, and hyperglycosylated hCG. Regular hCG is the predominant form associated with most pregnancies and non-invasive molar pregnancies, produced by trophoblast cells in placental tissue. Hyperglycosylated hCG is the main form during implantation, invasive molar pregnancies, and choriocarcinoma. Testing hCG levels can be measured in blood or urine, commonly for pregnancy detection. A positive hCG test indicates an implanted blastocyst and embryogenesis. hCG testing is also used to diagnose and monitor germ cell tumors and gestational trophoblastic diseases. Concentrations are reported in milli-international units per milliliter (mIU/mL). Blood tests, which are more sensitive than urine tests, can detect β-hCG levels as low as 5 mIU/mL. Reference Levels in Normal Pregnancy Serum hCG levels rise exponentially after conception and implantation. Quantitative β-hCG measurements are useful for monitoring germ cell and trophoblastic tumors, miscarriage follow-up, and ectopic pregnancy diagnosis. A lack of visible fetal structures on ultrasound at β-hCG levels above 1500 mIU/mL strongly suggests ectopic pregnancy, though viable intrauterine pregnancies are not excluded at levels above 2000 IU/L. Tumor Marker hCG can serve as a tumor marker, as its β subunit is secreted by certain cancers, including seminoma, choriocarcinoma, germ cell tumors, hydatidiform mole, and islet cell tumors. Elevated hCG in males may indicate testicular cancer, with normal levels ranging from 0–5 mIU/mL. Combined with alpha-fetoprotein, β-hCG is an excellent marker for monitoring germ cell tumors. Fertility hCG injections are widely used to induce final follicular maturation and ovulation in women undergoing fertility treatments. In men, hCG stimulates Leydig cells to produce testosterone, essential for spermatogenesis. It is also used to support the corpus luteum and enhance progesterone production in certain cases. Anabolic Steroid Adjunct hCG is used in conjunction with anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS) cycles to maintain and restore testicular size and testosterone production. Prolonged use of hCG at high doses can suppress endogenous LH production via negative feedback mechanisms. hCG Diet The use of hCG as an adjunct to ultra-low-calorie diets for weight loss has been discredited. Studies have shown no evidence that hCG enhances weight loss, alters fat distribution, or reduces hunger. The FDA has deemed hCG diet products fraudulent and ineffective. Homeopathic hCG Homeopathic hCG products, often containing no or negligible amounts of hCG, are marketed for weight loss but lack scientific validity. The FDA has classified these products as illegal and ineffective. Tetanus Vaccine Controversy Claims that tetanus vaccines in developing countries are laced with hCG-based anti-fertility drugs have been denied by the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF. Independent testing has found no traces of hCG in these vaccines.
